cards.statement: The Internet protocol suite groups protocols into link, internet, transport and application layers.
cards.explanation: RFC 1122 uses these four layers to organize Internet protocols and their host requirements.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers

cards.statement: IP repairs lost datagrams before passing their data to a transport protocol.
cards.explanation: IP provides a datagram service with no delivery guarantee. Higher layers supply reliability when needed.
cards.misconception: IP supplies reliable delivery.

cards.statement: In IPv4, ICMP belongs to the internet layer even though IP carries its messages.
cards.explanation: ICMP forms an integral part of IPv4; carrying ICMP inside IP does not make it a transport protocol.

cards.statement: An Ethernet MAC address with its M bit set identifies a group of recipients.
cards.explanation: The M bit in the first octet distinguishes group destinations, including multicast and broadcast, from unicast.

source.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol and Documentation Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters

cards.statement: The X bit set in an Ethernet MAC address marks an address from an IEEE-assigned global block.
cards.explanation: IEEE-assigned global MAC addresses have X equal to zero. X equal to one marks the local address space.
cards.misconception: A set X bit means universal assignment.

source.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol and Documentation Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters

cards.statement: RFC 894 sets 1500 octets as the maximum IP datagram length carried over Ethernet.
cards.explanation: Verified erratum 570 corrects 'minimum' to 'maximum' in RFC 894's Ethernet data-field limit.

cards.statement: ARP's address-resolution format requires an IPv4 address as its protocol address.
cards.explanation: ARP maps addresses of an indicated network protocol to hardware addresses. Its format is generic across protocol address spaces.
cards.misconception: ARP's format is specific to IPv4.

cards.statement: An Ethernet host broadcasts an ARP request when it lacks the target's address mapping.
cards.explanation: Broadcasting the ARP request lets the station holding the target protocol address receive the query.

cards.statement: An ARP target adds the sender's mapping after it checks that the opcode is a request.
cards.explanation: In RFC 826's reception algorithm, the target learns the sender's mapping before examining the opcode.
cards.misconception: An ARP target learns the sender after recognizing a request.

cards.statement: An IPv4 host uses ARP probes to check whether a candidate address is already in use.
cards.explanation: ARP probing checks for an address conflict on the link before the host starts using the candidate IPv4 address.

cards.statement: IPv4 stores the source and destination addresses as 32-bit values.
cards.explanation: Each IPv4 address occupies four octets in the IP header.

cards.statement: In an IPv4 /24 subnet, a host can take the all-zero host part as its unicast address.
cards.explanation: RFC 1122 does not permit an all-zero host part in an IPv4 address outside its listed special cases, so the .0 address of a /24 is not a host unicast address.
cards.misconception: The subnet address serves as an ordinary unicast host address.

source.title: RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

cards.statement: The IPv4 prefix /20 corresponds to the subnet mask 255.255.240.0.
cards.explanation: Twenty leading one bits select the prefix.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: An IPv4 /26 prefix contains 64 addresses before any host-use exclusions.
cards.explanation: Six host bits give 64 address combinations.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: In an IPv4 /24 subnet, a destination with an all-ones host part is the subnet broadcast address.
cards.explanation: The directed broadcast address selects the subnet rather than an individual host.

source.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

cards.statement: An IPv4 /31 point-to-point link reserves one of its addresses for directed broadcast.
cards.explanation: Both /31 addresses identify endpoints on a point-to-point link.
cards.misconception: A /31 retains a dedicated directed broadcast address.

source.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

cards.statement: CIDR selects an IPv4 prefix length from the address's legacy class.
cards.explanation: CIDR specifies prefix lengths explicitly instead of inferring them from address classes.
cards.misconception: Address classes still determine CIDR prefix lengths.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: The IPv4 prefix 198.51.100.0/25 contains the address 198.51.100.200.
cards.explanation: 198.51.100.0/25 spans last-octet values 0 through 127.
cards.misconception: The /25 covers the complete final octet.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: An IPv4 host uses its address and subnet mask to decide whether a destination shares its connected subnet.
cards.explanation: The host compares the masked destination with its own subnet prefix to choose direct delivery or a gateway.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers

cards.statement: The IPv4 address 172.31.255.1 belongs to the private-use block 172.16.0.0/12.
cards.explanation: The private-use /12 spans 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255.

cards.statement: IANA classifies 100.64.0.0/10 as an RFC 1918 private-use address block.
cards.explanation: 100.64.0.0/10 is Shared Address Space, allocated separately for uses involving carrier-grade NAT.
cards.misconception: Shared Address Space belongs to RFC 1918.

source.title: IANA-Reserved IPv4 Prefix for Shared Address Space

cards.statement: The IPv4 address 127.25.0.1 belongs to the loopback block 127.0.0.0/8.
cards.explanation: Loopback covers the entire 127.0.0.0/8 block, rather than just 127.0.0.1.

cards.statement: An IPv4 router may forward 169.254.0.0/16 traffic between its external interfaces.
cards.explanation: IANA marks 169.254.0.0/16 as link-local and not forwardable between a router's external interfaces.
cards.misconception: Routers forward IPv4 link-local traffic between links.

cards.statement: In IANA's IPv4 registry, a true Forwardable value marks a block as globally reachable.
cards.explanation: Forwardable concerns routing between external interfaces; Globally Reachable concerns forwarding beyond an administrative domain.
cards.misconception: Forwardable and Globally Reachable are equivalent flags.

cards.statement: An IPv4 host sends to 255.255.255.255 when it uses the limited broadcast destination.
cards.explanation: The limited broadcast destination reaches the connected network and does not pass through routers.

cards.statement: An author may use 198.51.100.0/24 for example IPv4 addresses in documentation.
cards.explanation: RFC 5737 reserves 198.51.100.0/24 for examples to avoid conflicts with assigned operational addresses.

source.title: IPv4 Address Blocks Reserved for Documentation

cards.statement: IANA makes 240.0.0.0/4 available for ordinary IPv4 unicast address assignments.
cards.explanation: IANA lists 240.0.0.0/4 as Reserved rather than as ordinary unicast address space.
cards.misconception: The reserved upper block is ordinary unicast space.

cards.statement: RFC 1918 lets operators propagate private-network routing information across inter-enterprise links.
cards.explanation: RFC 1918 says routing information about private networks shall not propagate on inter-enterprise links.
cards.misconception: Private routing information may cross inter-enterprise links.

cards.statement: A traditional NAT creates a mapping when an external host starts a session toward an unmapped private host.
cards.explanation: Traditional NAT sessions start from the private side. Inbound initiation uses a static mapping for a selected private host.
cards.misconception: Inbound initiation creates a traditional NAT mapping.

source.title: Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)

cards.statement: For UDP, RFC 4787 requires a NAT to reuse an internal endpoint's existing mapping across external endpoints.
cards.explanation: RFC 4787 requires Endpoint-Independent Mapping: the same internal address and port retain their mapping across external endpoints.

source.title: Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP

cards.statement: RFC 5952 formats hexadecimal letters in IPv6 addresses as lowercase.
cards.explanation: Canonical IPv6 text uses a through f; uppercase is accepted input but differs from the standardized output form.

source.title: A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation

cards.statement: RFC 5952 allows :: to shorten a single zero group in an IPv6 address.
cards.explanation: RFC 5952 reserves :: compression for runs of at least two zero groups; a lone zero group is written as 0.
cards.misconception: Canonical :: compression applies to a lone zero group.

source.title: A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation

cards.statement: IPv6 uses broadcast addresses to reach the nodes connected to a link.
cards.explanation: IPv6 replaces broadcast addressing with multicast addressing.
cards.misconception: IPv6 retains broadcast addressing.

cards.statement: An IPv6 host uses :: as a destination to reach its own protocol stack.
cards.explanation: :: represents an unspecified address. IPv6 uses ::1 for loopback delivery to the same node.
cards.misconception: The unspecified address also serves as loopback.

cards.statement: Each IPv6 interface has at least one link-local unicast address.
cards.explanation: Link-local addresses belong to fe80::/10 and serve communication on the attached link.

cards.statement: An IPv6 zone identifier selects the link for a link-local address on a host with several links.
cards.explanation: A zone identifier distinguishes which local link contains a link-local destination when the address alone is ambiguous.

source.title: Entering IPv6 Zone Identifiers in User Interfaces

cards.statement: An IPv6 Unique Local Address has link-local scope by default.
cards.explanation: Unique Local Addresses have global scope by default. Their scope does not imply global Internet reachability.
cards.misconception: Unique Local Addresses have link-local scope.

cards.statement: IANA currently limits IPv6 unicast address assignments to the range 2000::/3.
cards.explanation: IANA reserves the remaining global unicast address space for future definition and use.
cards.volatilityNote: IANA may revise which IPv6 address-space blocks are available for unicast assignments.

cards.statement: IPv6 sends a packet for an anycast address to the whole group of assigned interfaces.
cards.explanation: An IPv6 anycast packet reaches one assigned interface, chosen as nearest by the routing protocols' distance measure.
cards.misconception: Anycast delivers one packet to the entire group.

cards.statement: An author may use 3fff::/20 for example IPv6 addresses in documentation.
cards.explanation: RFC 9637 allocates 3fff::/20 for documentation alongside the earlier documentation space.

cards.statement: RFC 7136 treats an IPv6 interface identifier as a coded description of the interface's hardware address.
cards.explanation: RFC 7136 says the bits of an interface identifier have no generic meaning, and third parties must treat the whole value as an opaque bit string.
cards.misconception: Interface identifier bits encode hardware properties.

source.title: RFC 7136: Significance of IPv6 Interface Identifiers

cards.statement: A DHCPv4 client selects an offered address by identifying its chosen server in DHCPREQUEST.
cards.explanation: The Server Identifier option names the chosen server, allowing servers to recognize which offer the client accepted.

cards.statement: A DHCPv4 client in the rebinding state unicasts its DHCPREQUEST to the server that granted the lease.
cards.explanation: At T2, the client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST so any available server can extend the lease. Contacting the original server belongs to the earlier renewal stage.
cards.misconception: Rebinding contacts the original lease server just like renewal.

cards.statement: A DHCPv4 relay uses giaddr to tell the server which client subnet needs an address.
cards.explanation: The relay puts its address in giaddr. The server uses this field to identify the client's subnet when choosing an address.

cards.statement: An IPv6 host carries Neighbor Discovery messages in ICMPv6 when discovering routers and neighbors.
cards.explanation: Neighbor Discovery defines ICMPv6 messages for interactions between nodes on a link, including router discovery and neighbor address resolution.

source.title: RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)

cards.statement: An IPv6 host identifies its default router from the M flag in a Router Advertisement.
cards.explanation: A host learns default routers from Router Advertisements with a nonzero Router Lifetime. The M flag signals managed address configuration.
cards.misconception: The M flag selects the default router instead of signaling managed address configuration.

source.title: RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)

cards.statement: For IPv6 address resolution on a multicast link, a host sends Neighbor Solicitation to solicited-node multicast.
cards.explanation: A host directs the address-resolution query to the target's solicited-node multicast address.

source.title: RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)

cards.statement: For SLAAC, an IPv6 host trims its interface identifier to make an advertised prefix fit 128 bits.
cards.explanation: A host ignores a SLAAC Prefix Information option when prefix length plus interface identifier length differs from 128 bits; it keeps the link's interface identifier length.
cards.misconception: SLAAC adapts the interface identifier length to fit an arbitrary advertised prefix.

cards.statement: An IPv6 node may run Duplicate Address Detection on an anycast address before assigning it.
cards.explanation: IPv6 nodes must not perform Duplicate Address Detection on anycast addresses, which deliberately identify multiple interfaces.
cards.misconception: Duplicate Address Detection also applies to anycast addresses.

cards.statement: A DHCPv6 relay uses the client's UDP port 546 as its listening port for DHCPv6 messages.
cards.explanation: DHCPv6 clients listen on UDP port 546; servers and relay agents listen on UDP port 547. A relay follows the server-side listening role.
cards.misconception: A relay receiving client messages listens on the client port.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

cards.statement: A host uses stateless DHCPv6 to request an IPv6 address after processing a Router Advertisement.
cards.explanation: Stateless DHCPv6 provides only other configuration options, with no addresses or prefixes, so the server keeps no state. The host gets its IPv6 addresses by another mechanism.
cards.misconception: Stateless DHCPv6 provides IPv6 address leases.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

cards.statement: A DHCPv6 client can obtain a prefix to number networks on its downstream links.
cards.explanation: Prefix delegation gives the client address space to manage. The client can divide it into subnets and assign them to downstream links.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

cards.statement: An IPv6 receiver treats an ICMPv6 message with a type below 128 as an error message.
cards.explanation: ICMPv6 divides its type space into error messages below 128 and informational messages from 128 upward.

source.title: RFC 4443: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6) for the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Specification

cards.statement: In IPv4, a host must report a problem with a received ICMP error message by sending an ICMP error.
cards.explanation: RFC 1122 says a host must not send an ICMP error message as the result of receiving an ICMP error message, so a faulty ICMP error is never answered with another one.
cards.misconception: ICMP error messages receive further ICMP errors when they cause a problem.

source.title: RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: Classic traceroute sends successive probes with increasing IPv4 TTL values to reveal router hops.
cards.explanation: A router where a probe's TTL expires returns Time Exceeded. Increasing the TTL lets successive probes reach farther along the path.

source.title: RFC 2151: A Primer On Internet and TCP/IP Tools and Utilities

cards.statement: In IPv4, a router clears the DF flag before splitting a datagram that exceeds its next link's MTU.
cards.explanation: An IPv4 router discards a datagram that needs fragmentation when Don't Fragment is set. The bit prevents routers from splitting that datagram.
cards.misconception: Routers override Don't Fragment to forward oversized IPv4 datagrams.

cards.statement: An IPv4 router must be capable of forwarding a 68-octet IP datagram as one packet.
cards.explanation: The 68-octet forwarding minimum accommodates the largest IPv4 header plus one eight-octet fragmentation unit.

cards.statement: A filter that drops IPv6 Packet Too Big messages can let a TCP handshake succeed while data stalls.
cards.explanation: Small handshake packets may pass while larger IPv6 packets exceed the path MTU. Dropping Packet Too Big prevents the sender from learning the smaller MTU through ICMP-based discovery.

source.title: RFC 8201: Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6

cards.statement: An IPv6 router fragments an oversized packet before forwarding it onto a link with a smaller MTU.
cards.explanation: In IPv6, the source creates fragments and the destination reassembles them; routers leave fragmentation to the source.
cards.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets to fit the next link, as IPv4 routers can.

cards.statement: An IPv6 link must present an MTU of at least 1280 octets to hosts using the IPv6 layer.
cards.explanation: If the underlying link cannot carry 1280 octets in one piece, it supplies fragmentation and reassembly below IPv6 to meet the minimum.

cards.statement: A DPLPMTUD sender can treat a lost probe as proof that its size exceeds the path MTU.
cards.explanation: DPLPMTUD confirms a usable packet size from successful probe delivery. A lost probe may reflect congestion or a link error rather than an MTU limit.
cards.misconception: Probe loss conclusively identifies an MTU limit.

source.title: RFC 8899, Section 3: Features Required to Provide Datagram PLPMTUD

cards.statement: In ordinary IPv4 forwarding, a router replaces the destination IP address with its chosen next hop.
cards.explanation: Ordinary IPv4 forwarding preserves the destination IP address. The router uses a separate next-hop address to send the packet onward.
cards.misconception: Forwarding replaces the packet's destination with the next router.

source.title: RFC 1812, Section 5.2.4: Determining the Next Hop Address

cards.statement: In ordinary IPv4 forwarding, a router can let a lower-metric /16 outrank a matching /24 route.
cards.explanation: A matching /24 wins over a matching /16. The router selects the longest matching prefix before comparing route metrics.
cards.misconception: A lower route metric outranks a more specific matching prefix.

cards.statement: IPv4 routers can forward a reply along a different network path from the packet that prompted it.
cards.explanation: Routers make forwarding decisions independently at each hop. Routing in the reverse direction can lead through different routers.

source.title: RFC 1812, Section 5.3.8: Source Address Validation (asymmetric paths)

cards.statement: BGP speakers advertise IP prefix reachability between Autonomous Systems to build inter-domain routes.
cards.explanation: BGP shares reachable prefixes and paths across administrative boundaries.

cards.statement: A BGP speaker listens on TCP port 179 for the connections its peers open to start BGP sessions.
cards.explanation: BGP runs over TCP. RFC 4271 has every BGP implementation listen on TCP port 179 for incoming connections in addition to trying to connect to its peers.

cards.statement: BGP treats two peers in the same Autonomous System as external when they sit on different IP subnets.
cards.explanation: BGP peers in the same AS are internal peers, even across IP subnet boundaries.
cards.misconception: Subnet boundaries determine external BGP peering.

source.title: RFC 4271, Section 1.1: Definition of Commonly Used Terms

cards.statement: A BGP speaker appends its AS number to the right-hand end of AS_PATH when advertising to an external peer.
cards.explanation: A speaker advertising externally inserts its AS number before the existing AS_PATH.
cards.misconception: Speakers add their AS after the existing path.

cards.statement: A BGP speaker should exclude a route if its received AS_PATH contains the speaker's own AS number.
cards.explanation: The speaker's own AS in AS_PATH indicates a route has looped back.

cards.statement: A BGP speaker can use four-octet AS numbers to identify Autonomous Systems in route advertisements.
cards.explanation: The AS-number extension expands BGP's AS-number space beyond the original two-octet format.

source.title: RFC 6793, Sections 1 and 3: Four-Octet AS Number Extensions

cards.statement: Under RFC 8212, a BGP speaker lacking an explicit import policy for an EBGP peer considers that peer's routes eligible.
cards.explanation: RFC 8212 makes routes from an EBGP peer ineligible in the Decision Process until an explicit import policy is applied, though a speaker may offer an option to deviate.
cards.misconception: EBGP routes are used until an import filter is added.

cards.statement: UDP delivers an application's datagrams in the order in which the application sends them.
cards.explanation: UDP provides no ordering guarantee. A receiver may get datagrams in a different order.
cards.misconception: UDP guarantees datagram arrival order.

cards.statement: Each UDP base header has fields for source port, destination port, length and checksum.
cards.explanation: The eight-byte base header carries transport addressing, datagram length and checksum.

cards.statement: A UDP sender calculates its checksum independently of the source and destination IP addresses.
cards.explanation: The UDP checksum includes a pseudo-header containing the source and destination IP addresses.
cards.misconception: UDP checksum calculation excludes IP addresses.

cards.statement: UDP reduces an application's sending rate when the network becomes congested.
cards.explanation: Applications using UDP need congestion control in the application or a protocol above UDP; UDP itself supplies none.
cards.misconception: UDP supplies automatic congestion control.

cards.statement: TCP and UDP use 16-bit port numbers to distinguish services at an IP endpoint.
cards.explanation: The transport layer uses port numbers to direct incoming data to the intended application.

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: When IANA assigns a port to a service that asked only for UDP, it also assigns that number for TCP.
cards.explanation: Since RFC 6335, IANA assigns a port only for the transport protocols requested and marks the number Reserved for the others; older assignments often cover both.
cards.misconception: A UDP port assignment automatically includes TCP.

source.title: RFC 6335: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: IANA keeps the Dynamic Ports range outside the pool of port numbers available for service assignments.
cards.explanation: IANA makes no assignments in 49152–65535; applications use this range locally.
tags: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: An IANA port assignment allows an operator to prove the application protocol from the port number.
cards.explanation: An assigned port suggests a service, but its traffic can belong to a different application protocol.
cards.misconception: An assigned port proves which protocol its traffic uses.
tags: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

cards.statement: IANA assigns UDP port 123 to NTP traffic between time-synchronization endpoints.
cards.explanation: The registry lists ntp on UDP port 123, giving operators a standard destination to check for NTP.

source.title: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

cards.statement: A TCP server distinguishes clients sharing an IP address using their source ports.
cards.explanation: TCP identifies connections by both endpoints' addresses and ports.

cards.statement: A TCP sender counts its SYN as one sequence position even with an empty payload.
cards.explanation: Sequencing the TCP SYN makes retransmission and duplicate detection work during setup.

cards.statement: TCP should derive initial sequence numbers from a clock plus a keyed function.
cards.explanation: Keyed generation makes TCP initial sequence numbers harder to predict.

cards.statement: A TCP endpoint advertises its maximum outgoing TCP payload in the MSS option.
cards.explanation: A TCP endpoint advertises its maximum receivable payload in MSS.
cards.misconception: An advertised MSS describes the sender's transmit capacity.

cards.statement: After a TCP peer sends FIN, the other peer can still send data on that connection.
cards.explanation: TCP closes its sending directions independently, so one direction can remain open.

cards.statement: A TCP endpoint sends RST as the final confirmation of an orderly FIN exchange.
cards.explanation: A TCP RST aborts a connection, abandoning queued data rather than completing an orderly close.
cards.misconception: RST confirms a graceful FIN exchange.

cards.statement: A TCP peer in SYN-SENT may reject a valid peer SYN because both peers initiate the connection.
cards.explanation: TCP supports simultaneous open, letting two active peers complete connection establishment.
cards.misconception: Crossed SYNs force an active open to fail.

cards.statement: In a sequential TCP close, the peer that receives the first FIN takes the TIME-WAIT role.
cards.explanation: For an orderly TCP close, the first FIN sender takes TIME-WAIT as the active closer.
cards.misconception: The passive closer retains TIME-WAIT.

cards.statement: TCP must set its TIME-WAIT timer to twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime.
cards.explanation: TCP's TIME-WAIT lets delayed segments expire and retains state to acknowledge a retransmitted FIN after a lost final ACK.

cards.statement: A TCP implementation enables keep-alive probes by default for an idle connection.
cards.explanation: TCP keep-alives are optional; implementations that include them start with probing disabled.
cards.misconception: Keep-alive probing starts enabled.

cards.statement: A TCP receiver preserves the boundaries between separate writes made by the sending application.
cards.explanation: TCP transports bytes; receiving applications supply their own message framing.
cards.misconception: TCP preserves application write boundaries.

cards.statement: A TCP sender advances data sequence numbers by payload bytes rather than by segment count.
cards.explanation: Sequence positions track bytes across segmentation and retransmission.

cards.statement: A TCP receiver can use SACK to report received byte ranges separated by gaps in the data.
cards.explanation: SACK blocks describe received ranges, helping the sender avoid resending data that arrived.

cards.statement: A TCP sender replaces its smoothed round-trip estimate with the latest measured round-trip time.
cards.explanation: TCP blends new RTT samples with its existing estimate and includes variation when calculating its retransmission timeout.
cards.misconception: The latest RTT measurement replaces the running estimate.

cards.statement: TCP classic fast retransmit resends a suspected missing segment after three consecutive duplicate ACKs.
cards.explanation: The duplicate ACK pattern triggers retransmission before the retransmission timer expires.

cards.statement: A TCP receiver advertises its receive window to report the network path's capacity for more data.
cards.explanation: The receive window limits outstanding data according to what the receiving endpoint is prepared to accept.
cards.misconception: The receive window describes available network capacity.

cards.statement: A TCP sender uses the larger of its congestion and receive windows to limit outstanding data.
cards.explanation: The smaller of cwnd and rwnd governs outstanding data, respecting both limits together.
cards.misconception: The larger window determines the sending limit.

cards.statement: A TCP implementation must let an application disable the Nagle algorithm on an individual connection.
cards.explanation: Nagle coalesces small sends; applications have a connection-specific switch for that behavior.

cards.statement: A TCP receiver can deliver later bytes to the application while an earlier byte remains missing.
cards.explanation: TCP delays later application data until the gap is filled, preserving delivery order.
cards.misconception: TCP delivers application data beyond gaps.

cards.statement: A DNS client treats www.example.net. as a name relative to its configured search domain.
cards.explanation: The trailing dot represents the root label, so www.example.net. is an absolute name rather than a name to extend with a local suffix.
cards.misconception: A trailing dot leaves a DNS name relative to a search domain.

source.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities

cards.statement: A DNS server matches the ASCII names API.example.net and api.example.net as the same domain name.
cards.explanation: DNS comparison treats ASCII uppercase and lowercase letters as equivalent, even when a server preserves their original appearance.

source.title: RFC 4343: Domain Name System (DNS) Case Insensitivity Clarification

cards.statement: A DNS stub resolver hands a lookup to a recursive resolver to obtain the final answer.
cards.explanation: A stub resolver depends on a recursive resolver to perform the resolution work it lacks the capability to complete itself.

cards.statement: IANA describes the DNS root service as named authorities running across hundreds of servers.
cards.explanation: The root service spreads its named authorities over many server instances, rather than one machine per authority.
cards.volatilityNote: The number and distribution of deployed root-server instances can change.

cards.statement: A DNS resolver applies one response-wide TTL when caching records from the same reply.
cards.explanation: DNS gives resource records their own TTLs, so records from one response can have different cache lifetimes.
cards.misconception: A DNS response has a single cache lifetime shared by its records.

source.title: RFC 1035: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification

cards.statement: A DNS resolver keeps a record that arrived with a TTL of zero in its cache to answer the next query for that name.
cards.explanation: RFC 8767's TTL definition says a zero TTL limits a record to the transaction in progress and that the record should not be cached, not even for stale fallback.
cards.misconception: A zero TTL means the record never expires, as in some other caches.

source.title: RFC 8767: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency

cards.statement: A DNS resolver uses the SOA MINIMUM field alone to set a negative answer's cache lifetime.
cards.explanation: For NXDOMAIN and NODATA, the negative-cache TTL is the smaller of SOA MINIMUM and the SOA record's TTL.
cards.misconception: SOA MINIMUM alone determines the negative-cache lifetime.

source.title: RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)

cards.statement: A DNS resolver can serve expired cached records when it fails to refresh them from authoritative servers.
cards.explanation: Serve-stale permits a resolver to use expired data during a refresh failure, preserving answers through temporary authoritative-server outages.

source.title: RFC 8767: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency

cards.statement: A general-purpose DNS implementation must support TCP for queries as well as UDP.
cards.explanation: TCP support forms part of general-purpose DNS service, including ordinary queries; it is more than a transport for zone transfers.

source.title: RFC 7766: DNS Transport over TCP - Implementation Requirements

cards.statement: A DNS requester uses EDNS(0) to advertise how large a DNS response its TCP connection accepts.
cards.explanation: EDNS(0) advertises the requester's capacity for larger UDP responses, allowing them to remain on UDP instead of requiring a TCP retry.
cards.misconception: EDNS(0) advertises a TCP response-size limit.

cards.statement: A DNS server groups A and AAAA records with the same owner name into one RRset.
cards.explanation: A DNS RRset groups records with the same owner, class and type; A and AAAA belong to separate sets.
cards.misconception: Matching owner names merge different record types.

cards.statement: A resolver reads an IPv4 address from the RDATA of an AAAA record.
cards.explanation: An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address for its owner name.
cards.misconception: AAAA supplies IPv4 address data.

source.title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6

cards.statement: A zone administrator places a CNAME at the zone apex alongside its SOA and NS records.
cards.explanation: A zone apex holds SOA and NS records, which conflict with CNAME coexistence rules; DNSSEC records are the exception.
cards.misconception: A zone apex accepts CNAME alongside its required records.

cards.statement: A mail sender prefers a lower MX preference value when choosing among a domain's mail exchangers.
cards.explanation: MX preference ranks mail exchangers in ascending order, so smaller values get tried first.

cards.statement: RFC 2181 lets the host named in a domain's MX record be a CNAME alias that points to the mail server.
cards.explanation: RFC 2181 says an MX target must not be an alias but must have its own address records, because additional-section processing does not follow CNAMEs.
cards.misconception: An MX target may be a CNAME alias.

source.title: RFC 2181: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

cards.statement: A secondary DNS server compares its SOA serial with the primary's to detect a changed zone.
cards.explanation: RFC 1034 has secondaries poll the primary for the zone's SOA record; an advanced serial means the zone changed, so the secondary fetches a new copy.

source.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities

cards.statement: A domain administrator publishes an SPF policy as a TXT record at the domain name.
cards.explanation: SPF puts a sender-authorization policy in TXT data for the domain being evaluated.

source.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) for Authorizing Use of Domains in Email, Version 1

cards.statement: An IPv6 reverse-DNS lookup searches for PTR records beneath in-addr.arpa.
cards.explanation: PTR lookups for IPv6 addresses use the ip6.arpa reverse tree.
cards.misconception: IPv6 reverse lookups share IPv4's reverse tree.

source.title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6

cards.statement: An SRV-aware client learns the destination port from the service's SRV record.
cards.explanation: SRV data includes the service's port as well as its target host, so clients can use the advertised port.

source.title: A DNS RR for specifying the location of services (DNS SRV)

cards.statement: An authoritative DNS server guarantees a complete record listing in its response to an ANY query.
cards.explanation: An authoritative server may answer ANY with a small subset or synthesized response; ANY does not promise an exhaustive record listing.
cards.misconception: An ANY response guarantees an exhaustive record list.

source.title: Providing Minimal-Sized Responses to DNS Queries That Have QTYPE=ANY

cards.statement: Counting TLS alone, a basic full TLS 1.3 handshake lets clients send data after one round trip.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 clients send 1-RTT data after Finished.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 server gains cross-connection replay protection from 0-RTT record encryption.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 gives early data no cross-connection replay guarantee.
cards.misconception: Encryption prevents early-data replay.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 server encrypts its certificate during the handshake.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 encrypts Certificate with handshake keys.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: TLS 1.3 public-key exchanges provide forward secrecy for 1-RTT application traffic.
cards.explanation: Long-term-key compromise does not reveal previous traffic keys.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 endpoint negotiates a separate MAC algorithm for record protection.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 models every record cipher as AEAD, one operation that both encrypts and authenticates, so records need no separately negotiated MAC.
cards.misconception: Record protection negotiates a separate MAC.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 client sends ClientHello to renegotiate an established connection.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 forbids renegotiation on established connections.
cards.misconception: TLS 1.3 retains renegotiation.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: To negotiate TLS 1.3, a server reads the version the client offers from the legacy_version field of the ClientHello.
cards.explanation: A server negotiates TLS 1.3 only through supported_versions, and when a ClientHello carries that extension, the server must not use legacy_version for version negotiation.
cards.misconception: legacy_version still drives version negotiation when supported_versions is present.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 sender places its own certificate first in the transmitted chain.
cards.explanation: The first certificate identifies the peer being authenticated.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS client can put a server's literal IP address in the SNI host_name field.
cards.explanation: SNI host_name carries a DNS hostname; literal IP addresses are forbidden.
cards.misconception: SNI accepts IP literals.

source.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions: Extension Definitions

cards.statement: A TLS client accepting wildcards matches * in *.example.net against exactly one DNS label.
cards.explanation: A TLS wildcard for *.example.net covers api.example.net, rather than a.b.example.net.

cards.statement: A QUIC sender carries TLS handshake bytes in CRYPTO frames instead of TLS records.
cards.explanation: QUIC supplies its own framing and packet protection for TLS handshake bytes.

cards.statement: A QUIC server sends application data on a unidirectional stream opened by its client.
cards.explanation: The client sends data on its client-initiated unidirectional stream.
cards.misconception: The recipient sends stream data.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC receiver raises a stream's individual data limit by increasing its connection-level limit.
cards.explanation: QUIC tracks stream and connection limits separately; raising connection credit leaves the stream limit unchanged.
cards.misconception: Connection credit also increases the individual stream limit.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC sender can retransmit lost stream data using the original packet number.
cards.explanation: QUIC resends stream data in a newly numbered packet, making individual transmission acknowledgments unambiguous.
cards.misconception: Stream retransmission reuses its original packet number.

source.title: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control

cards.statement: A QUIC endpoint tracks Initial, Handshake and application data in separate packet number spaces.
cards.explanation: QUIC separates packet acknowledgments across these spaces; 0-RTT and 1-RTT share the application-data space.

cards.statement: A QUIC sender can choose CUBIC in place of the NewReno-like congestion controller.
cards.explanation: QUIC's congestion signals accommodate alternative sender-side algorithms; its specified controller is an example.

source.title: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control

cards.statement: A QUIC server bases its pre-validation amplification budget on the number of received packets.
cards.explanation: Before validation, a server limits outgoing bytes to three times received bytes.
cards.misconception: Amplification accounting counts packets.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC client must make the UDP payload carrying an Initial packet at least 1200 bytes long.
cards.explanation: The client pads or coalesces packets to meet this minimum.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC server's Version Negotiation packet selects the version for the client's next connection attempt.
cards.explanation: The packet lists offered versions. The client selects a mutually supported version for its new first flight.
cards.misconception: The server's packet chooses the retry version.

cards.statement: A QUIC sender must resend DATAGRAM frames when their packets are declared lost.
cards.explanation: QUIC's DATAGRAM extension leaves lost datagrams unretransmitted, even though their packets elicit acknowledgments.
cards.misconception: The QUIC transport retransmits lost DATAGRAM frames.

source.title: RFC 9221: An Unreliable Datagram Extension to QUIC
